All right, this is, as you probably can tell, the first tape of an extended interview with Mr. Charles Mingus, American composer.

Charles, you probably let us know more about yourself than virtually anybody in jazz. I mean, you've written a book, a rather celebrated book, Beneath the Underdog, and you've had very, very candid album notes that you've dictated or written. And you've had even a letter by your psychiatrist on the back of an album.

And it seems to me that we -- that for all that we know about Charles Mingus, that there are a great many unanswered questions, still, and I'd like to kind of develop those a little bit. For example, I really am curious to know what you meant by the title of your book, Beneath the Underdog.

Well, the underdog is obviously the black people. And I felt more beneath them than -- I felt beneath -- not only was the white man prejudiced to them, and I'm involved (inaudible) half-yellow shit-colored nigger, as I was called was even farther under the prejudice because it came from both sides, the white and the black.
See, I never fully understood that.
The blacks are not together, and they (inaudible) when I was a child. It was prejudiced against light skin, For instance, (inaudible) like Clayton Powell, who looks like a white man, they were

called elite. And they had the underground clan of the black who were school, in the knowledge of the history of the black people, the Africans, slaves, I never was taught anything about that, how they escaped. And they felt better (inaudible). So you call that the (highest) ECHELON of the black people. And they didn't associate with the common blacks, worked in labor and laborer or garbage men. Out in Watts, (inaudible) talking to guys whose parents weren't able to have an education, they couldn't hardly read or write. So I was in the middle of all of those, and I (inaudible) that I chose to decide to hang out with the outcasts, which was Japanese, Greek, Italian guys hang out and smoke cigarettes and drink wine against the building across from the schoolyard.
I think it's clear that I MEANT, beneath the underdog, beneath the black people. They're still more prejudiced -- you ever hear of a game called dung-pile power?
What was that?
Dung-pile power.
No.
They used to play a game where they run and jump on a guy, and everybody would pile on top of him. But I was always at the bottom of the game.
I was, too. We didn't call it the same thing, but I know the game very well.
There were 20 guys on top of you.
Yeah. You know, the irony is that one

time my sister was teaching retarded children, and she had me come by to make photographs for her school. And the kids -- they were mostly Mongoloid boys, and they were enormous.-- 13 or 14, but they were great, big kids already.

And so they hadn't seen a man in that place. All the counselors were women, and they really were turned on by having a man around. And they needed to, like, be rough and all that business with somebody, and so one of the teachers talked me into playing a game of touch football with those kids. And so the first thing I knew was, somebody tossed me the ball and before I could make a move, instead of touching, some of the kids came over and they started to try to knock me down, and I figured, well, I'll give them -- I'll fall down and make it seem real to them. And every single one of them, there must have been 20 kids, piled on top, before anybody could stop them. It took ten minutes to get them to get off. I mean, they were just having a wonderful time.
But it seems to me that that kind of pile-on attitude is -- there's something less than endearing about it. The --
In other words, I felt very persecuted by the white man and the black man. Who's supposed to do most of the talking, you or me?
I'm just wondering that. You're supposed to do the talking, Charles.
Well, (inaudible) be short as possible.
All right. The -- I know a little bit about some of the people who had an influence on you. But I just wonder if you could say again as to who they were and what they meant to you.

Jimmy Blanton was a great influence on me. I tried to learn what he did, but I knew it was complicated because nobody's played those type of intervals in jazz that I know of. As far as I'm concerned, (inaudible). So I tried to play the things he played, like Georgia Brown, "Jack the Bear," "Sophisticated Lady," "Jumpin' Pumpkin," (singing), what's that for blues -- blues, something. (Singing.) And Duke Ellington. He (inaudible) do that solo together "Jack the Bear"? Did I say Jackie Brown? "Jack the Bear," but say it again.
I think you may have said Jackie Brown, but say it again.

Whatever he did, I tried to learn. It was a different approach to the bass in jazz. Most guys go down one string, and slide into the next one, without using any of the positions across the instrument. To play the way he played, you had to do that way, to make speed, to get there in time. And Art Tatum was a definite influence, because I had to work with him and study with him for a duet he always told me he wanted to get. It was many years before I got to play with him in person, on a job which was in Miami, Florida, Birdland, I think it was. Bud Powell, I was never influenced, but I liked him. I liked his playing.

Having my ears come from Ellington, Charlie Parker. (Inaudible) I thought Charlie Parker's 2nd Bird was simpler, simpler to hear than Ellington, simpler than Art Tatum. I felt that guys who hadn't heard Duke Ellington, all the beboppers, for instance, or Art Tatum, would think that Charlie Parker was the most complicated, the most advanced lyrical lines going blowing in jazz. I never thought that.

That's the reason why the music I was playing was so different from Charlie Parker. Everybody else was playing bebop. Because I still thought there was something more important than just playing or writing tunes on the blues or some other tune with a different melody. Although Bird did play some hard (inaudible) compositions, I felt it was better if he wrote his own compositions, chord structure and all. Which most of the time he didn't. If he did do that, he did it to a blues structure. Which (inaudible) nobody, he has (inaudible) on the blues.

I liked Bird, but I don't think he influenced me that much. I was influenced by Ellington. Freddy Webster, I liked Freddy Webster's Pass the Barrel, although some people say that Pass the Barrel came from Bird. But according to Fats, Freddy Webster was already playing those type of lines that Bird was playing, before Bird was even heard of. (Singing.)
Which is not bebop, but that was the kind of lines I liked. Freddy playing with Jimmy Nelson's band. His sound was so big. He used to play the ballad Stardust. Little kids in the audience

who didn't know nothing about music, crying. Tears were in their eyes. Of course, mine was flowing, too. So I guess [one of] Freddy Webster (inaudible) on my influence, but I admired his playing and style of playing, especially since he's got such a beautiful sound, and so soulful.
Let's see, there must be somebody else. Yeah, Debussy. I used to hear his music a whole lot. (Inaudible.) "Images"
Yeah, that was Debussy.

Debussy? It was so long -- when I was young, (inaudible) what I listened to. (Inaudible) Bach, I never heard too much Bach when I was young. But I changed my direction when I heard (inaudible). Heard Richard Strauss, "Death and Transfigurations", Stravinsky, which I like very much, but I still like Debussy better, for my own kind of music. I (inaudible) Stravinsky, but if I had to choose between the two, I would choose Debussy.

I keep saying Ellington, although I didn't come into Ellington until after I come into Debussy. Because I was hanging with a piano player named Spaulding Givens when I was studying classical bass with Rheinschagen. He opened my ears to these other composers. We were thinking about being classical composers when we were young. We never knew there was anything in jazz, because DownBeat magazine was a thing that only covered New York musicians -- still is, I think, it's very prejudiced to the whole field of jazz, even though a fellow lives on the Leonard Feather

Coast. I haven't read a DownBeat for years, but I see every from Buddy Collette body collect what he's doing. You go in the studios, I'm told PLAYING DOWN THERE. Leonard Feather (inaudible). I saw that the last time I was on the Coast, with Phil Moore, and I was wondering why he doesn't write about the guys all over America. The book is so narrow, a few that danced out here guys (inaudible) in the cold, snow and the blizzards and rain. These are the only ones that (inaudible) get accepted by DownBeat.

So that didn't flatter me at all, because I was thinking about felt like to write doing symphonies. My whole dream was writing symphonies, Not thinking about ballets, opera, ballets. (Inaudible) "Purple Heart," for instance, which was a black and white thing. I decided to do that later [weren't going to get in] when I found out that blacks (inaudible) the symphony. Or [get the rap] getting it right from the operas.
It's kind of rough to say what I'm trying to say.
Doing very well.

I know what I said. Me and Spaulding Gibbons -- he called me Debussy, I called him Ravel, because I heard him play -- we was recording things on piano, and he sounded like Ravel to me. I sounded something like Debussy to him. (Inaudible) Before we realized that black people don't nothing for the get to play classical music or write (inaudible) symphony. on bass with Rheinschagen. Which I was studying for (inaudible). My dream was not to get a symphony orchestra to stay there, but we got to get in I figured I had to write something for them. there to play to get the (inaudible).
Yeah.

I didn't know it was two different routes, you were a writer -- you was a writer, it was cool, and you get in from that end. Oh, there's so many guys out there that write, too, like Phil Moore, Calvin Jackson, Benny Carter, they haven't got in yet, either. They get a lot of studio work, to ghost write for people. That's always available for people to do.

I remember, that was the first time I saw Jimmy Knepper, he was out to Dmitri Tiomkin's (inaudible). It was a big white house on -- what street was that on? Hollywood Boulevard? A bunch of kids (inaudible) know what they were doing? They all had a little project like taking one or two bars of his music and modulating to another key for eight bars, and he'd tell you how many bars you write, and getting prepared to go to -- if you're in D flat, like, an eight-bar modulation, you go into the key of C. And you get to moving, man, you blow some music.
Yeah.

You know? Although our teachers were the ones that sent us out there with experience. After I did it a couple of times, I said, 'What is Lloyd Reese getting paid for this?' And Phil Moore hasn't got great yet for film scores. And I know he did four scores for them. I don't mean everything, but 20 minutes to a half an hour of music.
Well, it's still the practice that goes on.
I guess This guy's got to do it, because they get so big, and so many movies, they can't do them all. God knows, Dmitri Tiomkin was quite capable of doing anything he wants to do.
Yeah.

I would say that (inaudible) influence on me, too, because I saw his name on so many films. I would listen to his music and buy some of his backgrounds that he wrote tried to play like (inaudible) Walter Page although I accepted him, because he was sliding on that one and I (inaudible) string. I never respected him too much, when I was younger. But I did understand that he did know what he was doing and he could swing, as I grew older. He did contribute to bass playing. (inaudible) Most bass players were playing like Walter Page, (singing), two notes. Jimmy Blanton used to come in playing, (singing). He would run the scale now and then, but (inaudible) you'd call it a melodic line, melodic walking line. Let me see who influenced me. I guess you could say Church, to an extent. Not that I was proud of it or anything. I remember when I was studying with Phil Moore one time, told me that he was -- it was a hot day in California and so the window was open, and you'd hear these church people out there singing real loud, Yonder Jesus Christ. And Phil scared me because he was an atheist. He said, "Why don't these bastards wake up? When they're dead, they're dead, dead and we're living, they're right where they belong. That's why (inaudible) because their mentality is so limited, OR somewhere else to go because they think that there's a heaven," I didn't want to get

in a fight with him because I thought there was a heaven also. Maybe that's why I'm so dumb, because I figure there's got to be something better than this. Where the game is not for real or for fair, that somewhere else there must be a game going on when you're doing something, with human beings that's for real for for fair, (inaudible) you're accepted and get a chance to do it. Why do you have to wait 25 years to record a composition? I'm still in the red on my record dates. I haven't made no money on the records yet.

It's unbelievable, because all my aspirations of have so much energy so I can youth are gone, to (inaudible) write all day long, so I did. That's how I lost all my wives. I was writing music. So I'm supposed to be resting up now, but Sue's got me going again, with several different things. I get a little rest.
Well, you're pretty well a self motivated man, I think. I don't think anybody can get you to do something they don't want to do.
I feel I got to do it now, anyway, to keep my health, my hands, together.
Yeah, it keeps you from sitting around, feeling sorry for yourself. Give yourself some work to do. Nothing wrong with that.
You once described yourself as a spontaneous composer.
Well, every second I'm not that, but every now and then I sit down at a piano and do some thing --- it

comes to my head, and not miss too many notes, I get away with it. On bass -- I'm talking about piano because my schooling was not that hip on piano. It was all my own fingering, most of it. I studied jazz piano with Lloyd Reese, and the scales weren't that hard, the scales. The proper fingering for the D minor or B minor because the fingering is different. I found my own system out, where the fingering was the same on the C scale as it was on the D flat scale. You can use the same fingers every time.
Yeah.
And I don't know how practical it is for anybody else, but I didn't think about the notes or what key I was in, when I did it that way. I just (inaudible) and play, by using the same fingers.
That makes a great deal of sense.
What?
It makes a lot of sense.
(inaudible) piano?
No, I never --
You never (inaudible) training, though.
Not much.
Spontaneous compositions. Maybe I can do eight bars (inaudible), but I think there are only so many of those you can do. And then they all end up sounding alike.
Yeah, you begin to look at yourself.

Yeah, you've got to sit down and study yourself and fool around in your head, what you want to play in your head and what you're able to play on the piano. At least, that's what I have to do, to get out of a rut.
Yeah.

I spend a whole lot of time just throwing away music. I found pieces I didn't like at all, and I wrote almost 24 bars, and never finished it, because I was trying to get out of something. Or I'd write something and at the Five Spot. finish it and leave it on the piano (inaudible). Like, I got two compositions -- I wrote my best compositions. One was called Dark Blackness and one was called Light Darkness. Light, you know. Dark Blackness, Dark Lightness, and Light Darkness. And it's something completely different, although most of my things are completely different. Maybe that's why, because of the stuff that I throw away in between gets rid of the connection.

Then there's a piece like Revelations, where I write every note and take my time, get everything down I wanted. And then turn around and do the six-eight, and do the same because of the notation, the guys don't even know it happened. thing in four-four. (Inaudible.) Have you seen that score?
I don't know if I have, no.
Well, ask Gunther Schuller (inaudible) to let you see it. Because when I first started that theme, (singing), six-eight theme, I didn't know it was possible to write it in four-four.
But I tried and got it done. Converted it and had it come out sounding the same.
Yeah.
Other than making it a swing beat Going Against It (inaudible).
When you were very interested in super-imposing meters, not just changing time signatures, but, like, you used to go into -- start playing in six against four.
Yeah.

And three and all kinds of changes while people were trying to play -- well, you went through another -- the other side of the coin, too, from spontaneous composition, in that period when you were with Teo Macero T.O. Vessero and the real Workshop, the Jazz Workshop, was named after, I guess. I remember, I think you were quoted by somebody as saying, "Write it out, write it out." Mingus means And so you just insisted that everybody in that group write everything that they were feeling out and not leave anything to chance or not try to fake anything. And so I guess you covered both ends of the spectrum.

Yeah. That's when I had that superb energy to want to do something like that. Because it wasn't just talk to say -- to do a operatic ballet, with tap dances from the Baby Laurence (inaudible) era. And -- well, in those times, Melissa Hayden from the classical dance era, Katherine Dunham from the modern
dance era. It wasn't just for fun I was saying that, just to talk. I really wanted to do it, but I couldn't ever get anybody with enough foresight to WANT TO get together and do it.
Yeah.

Katherine Dunham was going to help me for a while (inaudible). Because I'm not a dancer. I could tell her the story and she could do the choreography. I spent a lot of time with her, thinking we were going to do something together. But she had more things on her mind than to want to (inaudible) help me through my [You know, ballet people] ballet, my operatic ballet. (inaudible) would do a dance and sing at the same time, we wouldn't have to worry about classical voices other than the role of the elite white person. That voice represented them. But I was going to use street voices, ordinary voices, hot dog man, selling hot dogs, or saying, "Crawfish, get your crawfish," if you're in that neighborhood. First time I heard that (inaudible) was in Washington, D. C. All through the South, they sell crawfish.

I'm just trying to say that I ended up doing something that was just about one half of what I really wanted to do, what I was capable of doing. So you get into a rut, of just doing the simplest things. (inaudible) Maybe this illness that's on me now is 'cause I'm going to get my solfege together, got to really get my ears together and got to be able to say what I want -- what I hear in my head. I haven't got the complete use of my arms, like I should have. It's going to come back,
I imagine, if I live.

You once said something very interesting to me, at a time we were working on the Let My Children Hear Music album. The tape you've given me to transcribe on "The Shoes of the Fisherman's Wife," it wasn't a very good quality tape and there was some cuts in it or something like that. And I couldn't tell what the end of the melody was, the opening theme, from the tape.

And so I called you up when you were living on 5th Street, and I went over, and asked if you'd play it for me on the piano. And so you started (singing), and you played it about three times, and everything you played it, it came out -- it was pretty much the same but it came out in a different place. You just -- it was essentially the same theme, but you developed it a little differently every time, and it would come out -- it was the same number of bars --
(Singing.) "CHICAGO, CHICADO"

Yeah, or (singing), and you -- and so I said, I sort of -- you finally said, "Well, take it -- go back and listen to the record and figure out exactly what I did, because I don't remember exactly what was it I wrote." And you said, "If I could I wouldn't have any need to write any new music if I walked around with my head full of all the things I've already written."
I wouldn't. I wouldn't, maybe some

other people would. I always try to forget it. It's because I read a book by Debussy called The Mad Hatter. He used to be a critic in France. He couldn't work because everybody called him a radical and crazy, so he got a job as a critic and he reviewed other guys' music. And he don't like nobody, man.

But I remember one of the articles he was writing, he said, 'This guy really loves his music. He listens to himself so much he writes the same symphony every time.' So I'm not as good as he is, so when I write it, it all sounds like junk to me, so I throw it away and forget about it. And if I do steal it, I don't know about it. But he says he tries to forget it as soon as he can. Don't clutter your mind up with your own compositions.
Get the book. The Mad Hatter.
Yeah, as a matter of fact, I will. I've heard about that book.

Because the Duke said essentially the same thing. He said that he had to write his own music because he couldn't remember or didn't care about learning anybody else's, when he tried to get into a bunch of other things, and he found that that wasn't his talent. He just wasn't interested in developing that, and so he became an original composer. And he -- you once said another interesting thing to me, that during the same period, when we were talking about the

orchestration or something. You said, 'to cover up the bones' -- that you wanted to cover the skeleton of the music, because you didn't want anybody to figure out how you did it, or something like that. And I wonder if that was a motivation to -- some of the densities that you worked with, where things got real intense, and layer layer layer later and later and later. be very concerned that somebody like

Yeah, I used to (inaudible) Miles Davis was stealing what I was doing before I got it done myself. And he did. He did. He was a bebopper and Max Roach (inaudible) Bohemian Club and I was playing those extended chords, one chord pedal points. And Miles said, (inaudible) his language was, 'Motherfucker, what you doing playing one chord for a whole hour?' I said, 'Well, man, not really.' I said, 'I went to the bridge after 40 bars, or 50 bars, sometimes 60.' Said, 'We have a conductor to give a cue on that.' A conductor? There's no conductor there, motherfucker.' Said, 'You and your fucking ...' I said, 'Well,' band, you (inaudible) my drummer... No, then it was my piano, my piano player Mal Waldron gave us when (inaudible) was a cue. Well, I feel that it has gone far enough, with the development of one chord. And then, he gives his cue and we go to another part. Another movement in the piece.

Well, the proof I have of this, there's a society in Paris called the Charles Cross -- Charles de Cross, it's an award they give you, like an Oscar. I got several of those, about 2 or 3 of them. But I remember when Miles Davis first started playing one chord,

that's about ten years after I was doing it. He got an award from them. I got one, too, on the same piece, but my piece was written ten years before his. So I listened to Miles, I never heard him. It was just like the one I'd done, 'Blue Sea.' Either Blue Sea or -- one of those things that was on the album, 'Pithecanthropus Erectus,' where I used one chord.

I never felt confident with guys -- (inaudible) although the jazz did need some -- they were so hung up with playing, (inaudible) trying to play Charlie Parker, it was a good idea to come in with my one chord. Even Bill Evans in my band, wasn't doing that. Bill Evans came up there, and he didn't like to play with one chord at all. That's why he split. But then I wrote -- Brandeis University, when I did Revelations, I wrote it out for him. He had to do it. And he said, 'Man, I got to think about what you're doing. It looks pretty important.' He doesn't do it now, though, does he? But he did it with Miles Davis. He's the one that showed Miles, he and Wynton Kelly. One time they both of them did it in a band, Miles finally went for the extended chords.

Well, after his ex-pause out there (inaudible) the kind of Blue record was really cause expose it to Bill, was the fact that Bill could do that very well, and was into all the modes and all that business of the scales.

(Inaudible) He wasn't into it until he came into my band. Just my band, Bill was a great reader and has full of knowledge is a great man with harmony. I remember the first record, the piano player didn't show up,

so I called Bill, an emergency, and he was asking all about it. I said, 'Well, you can play any kind of passing fancy chords you want, long as it has a pedal on this chord here.' (inaudible). That was for Bethlehem Records. It was (singing), Hello, Mom. I don't remember the names of them, but there was talking on the record. You remember that one?
(Inaudible.) Probably.

"Every Time I Come Downtown," that one, "" and Celia, Celia was the one that had the one chord. Of course Bill could do it, because he's a thorough musician. But it took some explaining to get him to do it.
Yeah.

Because he wanted to go home. See, he didn't want to do anything I wouldn't like. I said, 'Well, so man, you got one chord, doesn't mean you play one chord with the same voicing every time. I said, 'Use the passing chords.' He was (inaudible) said, 'Why don't you write it out for me?' I said, 'It will take you years to write that out.' I said, at Duke; 'Look, when he plays the blues, he plays a different set on every chord change -- on every blues sequence.' He said, 'I haven't heard Duke "" you listen Gonzales, you'll hear (inaudible) do that. So he was behind Paul Gonzalez (inaudible), because he would do something different every 12 bars, him do that, when he comped, man, and never repeat himself. And Bud Powell can do that Duke is very underrated, (inaudible) man.
Oh, was it pianos? as a pianist? Yes, I agree with that.
Especially (inaudible). as a comer, to feed you. John Lewis is a good comer.
The records with Bird. He was just superb on those.

Funky. People don't think of John Lewis as being funky, but he's very funky. Funny (inaudible) Well, we're still on the question of who influenced me, who my favorite musicians were. I didn't get into Beethoven until much later, see, when I found out he was black. See, I didn't know he was black, a black German. Everybody don't know that, so when I found out he was one of the first black men to play music, I started listening at him, and I didn't like his orchestral writing until the later things he did, opus twelve. later, (inaudible). But his string quartets really got to me, especially nine, ten, eleven and twelve, round there. (inaudible) Because he was contrapuntal, he was everything, even though he couldn't hear with his physical ear.
Yeah.
Yeah. He heard inside, insight, you know that.
Sure did.
And that's what like I do now. That's hard, many to hear all that and do it that's hard. (Inaudible) with a pencil.

Well, it's having to fight the little -- that can stimulate the creative process, too. I mean, you said one time if things had been easy for you, you probably never would have turned out to be the kind of musician and person that you turned out to be.
Yeah, but that's because I didn't know
what kind of person I am.
What kind are you?

I don't know, man. I'm just out there looking at the facts, that I make a record date, I'm doing what I want to do, and all of a sudden I get the bill from Atlantic Records for $40,000, for the cost of the musicians. And I'm not getting but four or five myself. When am I going to make some money? I'm trying to find out where (inaudible) Joan -- what's her name, Joan what? Gets $600,000 in advance.
Joanie Mitchell.

Yeah, she gets $600,000 in advance. And it's only because I'm black, man. I had a record date I got you for, was supposed to do, (inaudible) for Columbia, remember the one [real]. with (singing), the thing I wrote, the one I did for them.
"Hobo Home."

Anyway, Illinois Jacquet I don't know if Jackie was supposed to remember him from " Flying Home." And he called me one day and said, "I'm not going to make it, man. They promised to give $1,000. See, because Gerry Mulligan and those guys get ten times the money we do. So they get $10,000 on a record date." I said, "Well, this is my date, man. I just want you to sit in and play the Flying Home thing." He said, "No, I'm not going to do it because those people have got to start paying us some money." He says, "Today, I'm going to get my own record company," and that's what he's doing, he's putting
his own records out. It hurt me, because the tune was built around him, Flying Home." And even though Dizzy Gillespie's tenor player --
You're right, he did a very good job. James Moody, is
(Inaudible.) He's a great player.
It is not was what I was thinking about. So I wrote, "There I go, there I go," and it didn't come to me be the same thing.
See, I never knew that -- that's the first that I really knew about what that tune was all about.

I was there, and waved my arms at the orchestra and all that, Illinois Jacquet before. but I really never knew about (Inaudible) That was a great piece. m. That was For Him. And what was so strange about it

(Inaudible) was that my cousin, Fess Fritz Williams' son, named Phil Williams, he works without a name. (Inaudible) he got two houses, because Fritz Williams just gave him the connections he had for all the black clubs. He (Inaudible) the black clubs and makes pretty good money, and steady, he works all the time. He's able to have himself two big houses, three now that his father has died. And he Illinois Jacquet told me that Yellow Jacket wasn't doing so well. He wasn't getting Jackie work. Jacquet
So I thought I was going to help Jackie (Inaudible) to pay attention to him again, by putting something good around him, from when he really was on tenor saxophone. But, you know --
Well, people are their own worst
enemy, sometimes.
Yeah. (Inaudible) on the Royal Suite. Like even Roy Eldridge, man; "Little" Changed his mind at the last minute.
Well, Jon Faddis did a good job, but it wasn't as a matter of fact, John the same as having Roy.

Well, the best I ever played was Oscar came to San Francisco with Duke and Vern Ellis (inaudible) jam session.
Uh-huh.
(Inaudible), but I played exceptionally well.
Who were the other players?
Nobody but me.
Oh, I see, yes. Do you remember any times when there were contests, that you were exceptionally good?
No, I wasn't in -- the best ever was Jimmy Blanton, Sam Stuart, Red Calendar (inaudible), just no competition.
You mean in terms of Blanton?
What we was doing.
Yeah. That's what I wanted to ask you about. I only heard him on records, I never heard him live. Why was Blanton so important? What was he doing that nobody had done before?
(Inaudible.)
Anything else beside that?
Well, a lot of guys -- see, like, Eddie Gomez, they can (inaudible), but they don't. They only play up high. Some musicians (inaudible), but Jimmy Blanton played up high and down low, (inaudible).
And the guys before him, aside from covering the whole instrument, I guess -- was their rhythm different than Blanton? Did he loosen up the rhythm?
(Inaudible) by Walter Page.
Did you get to talk to --
Very little technique. Just sliding down the strings.
Jazz bass players made the bass (inaudible).
Yeah.
There are some classical bass players who are out there by themselves -- I forgot their names. Like __________, who was a beginner playing bass (inaudible).
I know. When I was a kid, I got some recordings of his, solo bass, and compared it to Blanton, to you, to Scott Lethero, it was like kindergarten.
It was written in G, played in the key of G and the key of D minor. That was about it. Playing the keys that are simple for bass.
Yeah.
Blanton played in all keys, in D flat, G flat, B natural.
But you were saying that you enjoyed playing bass when you were coming up. What sort of -- when did the enthusiasm begin to lessen to some extent?
It lessened (inaudible) I wasn't interested in going with the guys.
Yeah.

Because there was nowhere to blow. And (inaudible) with Charlie Parker in __________. That was a long time ago. I remember, the first time I saw him -- the second time I saw him put somebody down. G. G. Grace was
that.

Yeah. I remember that night at Birdland. You were in the band and Max and Bud Powell and I think Kenny Durham. And there was that awful business with -- he started yelling for Bud to get on the stand.
That wasn't Max. That was Art Blakey.
Art Blakey, right, yeah. And I remember, you were trying to bring some sanity to the whole thing, but finally --
I thought I was. I shouldn't have said nothing.
Why?
Not as crazy as he was.

Well, he seemed so that night. But did he seem a tragic figure to you? At times? Because, I remember one night, I was coming downstairs and as I said, I barely knew him. But he was going upstairs, tears going down his eyes, and he said, I've got to see you, I've got to see you tomorrow. And he looked so sad.
There's a picture of him and Bud Powell that night, and -- have you seen that way, where Bud was laying in arms?
No.
And Bud looks like a puppet. I don't know where that picture -- this is (inaudible). They both
playing classical music.
I did that, too, yeah. I used to do a classical show, where I played the music first, before I'd tell who the composer was or the performer.
I always thought you'd be a good disc jockey because you ears for that.
Yeah, well, --
You hear jazz.
What about (inaudible)? I mean, you've had a fair amount to say about the whole business of jazz. Has either one of them or both of them done something good in terms of the jazz musician?

(Inaudible), I never worked for him. When Billie Holiday demanded that he hire me because (inaudible), I did the first jazz philharmonic cheap because he's (inaudible). To work for nothing, because these two guys (inaudible) money. With George ______, they never paid enough money, man. Just before I got sick, I was able to find some agents who paid enough money. (Inaudible) ten dollars a concert. George ______ would have laughed if anybody asked for that kind of money.
That's interesting, because thre are classical musicians, and not only the very famous ones, the ones who are coming up, who get $10,000 a concert, but very few jazz people have ever done that.

No. He's a very dishonest man, and his wife -- he and his wife made millions of dollars off of hiring unknown musicians out in the sticks for little or no money, promise them one salary, get them out on the road and says, Lionel Hampton has the right to promise that kind of money. I was promised -- Lionel guaranteed me $400 a week when I first joined the band. And so I got on the road, I was very far away from California, and Hampton called to me and he says, why, we could pay that kind of money. No one -- Milt doesn't get that kind of money. But they didn't do that until they took us on the road. I kept getting these small checks, I said, what is this? $125 a week on the road.
Gee, and you had to pay your other stuff besides.
That's right.
That was his wife Gladys, as I remember.
They never paid me for arrangements, Mingus Fingers or nothing.
Maybe that explains why he's a Republican. He's the only jazz musicians that's ever campaigned for Nixon and Ford or those people.
He's Rockefeller's man.
I'm sure he believes in free enterprise.
and sat in at the -- Mingus' Friends in Concert.
Oh, yeah.
He came and sat in.
Yeah. What about his -- you were talking about Miles. How do you feel about Dizzy's work as it's gone through the years, his playing?
Well, Dizzy himself, after he started playing like Charlie Parker on trumpet --
Yeah.
He (unintelligible) from that. He progresses in what he's doing. Because he loves to play, loves to play trumpet. I guess he loved what Bird did.
Yeah.
But Freddie Russell was the ______.
Now, that's interesting, tell me that. I used to hear him on some of the -- there was a Sarah Vaughan record, but I've never heard him live. And I've heard several people say what you just said.
Well, Freddy Russell was the one that Dizzy copied. He was doing those things before Bird, according to ______.
Yeah.
And Miles loved him, Miles, Dizzy, all of them (unintelligible) Freddy. I heard Freddie in person. (Unintelligible) playing Stardust. I'll never forget
it, man. There were people in the audience, crying.
No kidding. What band was this?
Jimmy Lumsford.
What about the --
It was a big sound, another one of those big sounds.
Yeah. And what was he doing that anticipated what was to come? His harmonies were more complicated --
And his phrasing.
Yeah.
His form of phrasing. That's what Bird was doing so (inaudible). Dizzy was playing like Roy Hutchinson before he played like Bird.
Yeah.
(Unintelligible.) It's like, Lionel Hampton has recorded some music, and he's still playing that old-fashioned phrasing.
Yeah.
And it really sound like scales. And some embellishments embedded in the scales.
Yeah.
I wrote you a letter about that.
Yeah, I remember that.
Where the latest line was -- you
remember that? (Unintelligible) got me playing four-four.
Right.
What this suggests to me is Hampton.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
You ought to read that letter again.
Yeah.
You still go that letter?
I got a batch of them somewhere, yeah.
Yeah, you ought to read that letter.
Fats Dinero is obviously a figure in your book. My sense of it is that in terms of the histories these days, people tend to either ignore him or underestimate him. How important --
Fats?
Yeah. You'll see his name, but he doesn't get the space that he should get. How important was he?
Well, it's hard to tell, man, it's hard to say what a guy is giving. Like, Clifford Brown came out of (unintelligible).
Right.

More than he did out of Dizzy. Fats was warm in his playing. And he had all the tricks, he had all the embellishments, he had -- I remember, he told a story. See, when Bird and them was coming up, they were talking to
He has no -- my last date, there was no feeling.
In other words, even when the leader is somebody as strong as you are, if you can't counter effectively an A&R man who acts like that --
No. I brought Tio Too Muchord in because he knew scores, every score, and he don't have influence on . He couldn't work with him. I told Tio I was paying him myself.
Yeah. Couldn't you complain to Nessely?
Nessely doesn't have anything to do with the company anymore.
Oh, really? Oh, he's upstairs.
(Unintelligible) play last time.
Yeah.
And I hurt his feelings.

Oh, Mamarigloo, yeah. Gee, that's something I haven't thought of, that a guy who by now has the statute you have, is nonetheless forced, if you want to make the record on that label, to take an A&R man who he'd really rather not have.
That's right. And the rock and roll people take months, sometimes years, to record one record. And they expect us to go and do it in one or two days.
I'm talking about using music.
Yeah.
He should read the score and know what instruments to bring up at the time.
Yeah.
And they don't make them like that no more.
Yeah, I haven't been interested in --
(Unintelligible) with Columbia Records, and Tio was there, he could read (inaudible).
Was that Plout, do you know, that --
Big fellow?
Big guy, did a lot of classical dates, yeah.
Yes.
Yeah, he was fantastic. But you say it's not the same now.
Not where I am.

If you had the chance to -- if somebody gave you a grant, to make some records, and you'd be in charge of the whole operation in terms of picking the label, picking the studio, the A&R, the engineer, what would you do?
I'd get Teddy Charles.
Yeah.
Tio-Becelle, I'd get Teddy Charles for
an A&R man.
Yeah.
I'd get Tio Becelle for engineer, (inaudible) written music. I'd get Les Paul for the engineer.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
I'd get some guy who knows electronic things. I'd try to get the guy who's in Columbia.
Fred Plout, yeah.
What was his name?
His last name, I think, is Plaut, P-l-a-u-t. I'm not sure that Fred is his first name.
Yeah.
And where would you do it?
Church, that's where I'd go.
Church?
Church.
Yeah.
Columbia's church.
Oh, on 30th Street or something like that.
Yeah.

segments.chapter: Opening and early influences
segments.title: Opening of the Smithsonian interview with Sy Johnson
segments.summary: Smithsonian oral history, Washington, February 1978; Johnson introduces Mingus and his book Beneath the Underdog.

segments.chapter: Opening and early influences
segments.title: What Beneath the Underdog means; prejudice from both sides
segments.summary: Mingus explains the title: prejudice from whites and from light-skin-despising blacks, hanging out with outcasts; the dung-pile game and Johnson's own story.

segments.chapter: Opening and early influences
segments.title: Influences: Jimmy Blanton and Art Tatum
segments.summary: Mingus tried to learn Blanton's melodic bass lines and Ellington solos; he studied and rehearsed with Art Tatum.

segments.chapter: Opening and early influences
segments.title: Charlie Parker, Ellington and Freddy Webster as influences
segments.summary: Parker seemed simpler than Ellington to him, so his own music differed from bebop; he admired Freddy Webster's big sound.

segments.chapter: Opening and early influences
segments.title: Debussy, Ravel, Stravinsky and the dream of writing symphonies
segments.summary: Classical listening, studying bass with Rheinschagen, friendship with Spaulding Givens, DownBeat's neglect, and the barrier to black symphonic writers.

segments.chapter: Opening and early influences
segments.title: Studio writers and the Tiomkin assignments
segments.summary: Phil Moore, Calvin Jackson and Benny Carter ghost-write; Mingus and Jimmy Knepper do modulation exercises at Dmitri Tiomkin's house, taught via Lloyd Reese.

segments.chapter: Opening and early influences
segments.title: Walter Page versus Blanton, and Phil Moore the atheist
segments.summary: Page's two-note lines against Blanton's melodic walking; church singing and Phil Moore's atheism.

segments.chapter: Opening and early influences
segments.title: Writing all day, lost wives and keeping his hands together
segments.summary: Mingus says writing cost him his wives, Sue keeps him working, and he needs it for his health.

segments.chapter: Composing methods and more influences
segments.title: Spontaneous composition, piano fingering and throwing music away
segments.summary: His own piano fingering system, discarding pieces, and notating the six-eight theme of Revelations in four-four.

segments.chapter: Composing methods and more influences
segments.title: Superimposed meters, the Workshop and the operatic ballet idea
segments.summary: Writing everything out in the Workshop era, plans for an operatic ballet with Katherine Dunham and street voices, and his unrealized ambitions.

segments.chapter: Composing methods and more influences
segments.title: Forgetting his own compositions; the Shoes of the Fisherman's Wife tape
segments.summary: Johnson recalls transcribing a theme Mingus played differently each time; Mingus cites Debussy on not cluttering your mind with your own music.

segments.chapter: Composing methods and more influences
segments.title: Covering the bones, and Miles Davis's one-chord pedal points
segments.summary: Duke's comment on his own writing, Mingus hiding the skeleton of his music, and his claim that Miles borrowed his one-chord approach.

segments.chapter: Composing methods and more influences
segments.title: Bill Evans in the Mingus band and one-chord comping
segments.summary: Evans filling in on a Bethlehem date, learning to vary voicings on one chord, and comparison with Ellington and John Lewis.

segments.chapter: Composing methods and more influences
segments.title: Beethoven: discovering he was black, and the string quartets
segments.summary: Mingus came to Beethoven late, after learning he was black, and loves the late quartets.

segments.chapter: Composing methods and more influences
segments.title: Record debts and advances paid to others
segments.summary: Atlantic bills him $40,000 for a date while a pop singer gets a $600,000 advance; he blames race.

segments.chapter: Composing methods and more influences
segments.title: Illinois Jacquet, Flying Home and the Royal Suite trumpeter
segments.summary: Jacquet backs out of a Columbia date built around him; the cousin Phil Williams; Roy Eldridge changes his mind about the Royal Suite.

segments.chapter: Composing methods and more influences
segments.title: Duke Ellington, Billy Strayhorn and Lush Life
segments.summary: Mingus sees everything as Duke; he was in the bar while Strayhorn composed Lush Life.

segments.chapter: Composing methods and more influences
segments.title: Teachers and colleagues: Red Callender, Buddy Collette, Phil Moore
segments.summary: Callender, Collette and Phil Moore's arranging lessons (synthetic violin sound with French horn); Dizzy's debt to Bird.

segments.chapter: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
segments.title: Origins of pedal points and Jelly Roll Morton
segments.summary: Mingus on pedal point and what jazz is, learning of Morton's precedent, Miles years later, and the Debussy-like tags in his pieces.

segments.chapter: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
segments.title: Blind Tom and whether Erroll Garner could read
segments.summary: Memory pianists; Mingus disputes that Garner could not read, citing Garner's brother.

segments.chapter: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
segments.title: Lloyd Reese's way of teaching
segments.summary: Reese made them listen to Stravinsky and name the instruments, predicting Mingus would be an arranger.

segments.chapter: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
segments.title: Boyd Raeburn's band and Harry Babasin
segments.summary: Mingus was in Raeburn's band, threw down his bass over a syncopated part, recommended others, and never lasted with leaders.

segments.chapter: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
segments.title: Lionel Hampton years, Mingus Fingers and the bebop song
segments.summary: Hampton and Red Norvo were the longest jobs; tunes written for Hampton, lost in a bus wreck, and a bebop lyric Hampton disliked.

segments.chapter: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
segments.title: A New Haven concert with Benny Goodman, Hampton and Mel Powell
segments.summary: Johnson recalls hearing Mingus in a joint Goodman-Hampton concert; Mel Powell's turn to classical music.

segments.chapter: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
segments.title: Playing with Red Norvo and Tal Farlow
segments.summary: Johnson recalls Mingus dominating the trio; Mingus on Norvo's stiff beat and music he wrote for the group.

segments.chapter: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
segments.title: Monterey music, Eclipse, Portrait and Spaulding Givens
segments.summary: Johnson praises the Monterey music; Mingus plays records of Eclipse and Pink Topsy and praises Givens as an arranger.

segments.chapter: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
segments.title: Debut Records and keeping control of his publishing
segments.summary: Mingus ran his own label and publishing because he saw what happened to others.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Ending the first session and starting the next day
segments.summary: Mingus tires after about an hour; they stop, then resume for another session.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Rehearsing with Art Tatum and his harmonic ideas
segments.summary: What he learned from Tatum: richer progressions, such as his Night and Day changes and his dissatisfaction with the bridge.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Revoicing a childhood tune on piano
segments.summary: Mingus sings a children's song he always revoiced, putting six chords in it.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Early compositions of 1943 and having no favorites
segments.summary: Miss Bliss and other early pieces written in California; his favorite is always the next one.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Eclipse, The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady, and the Vanguard band
segments.summary: Johnson asks about the Black Saint album; Mingus says a working band for three months let the music be played right.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: The Town Hall concert fiasco and the ten-piece Vanguard band
segments.summary: Mingus blames promoters for turning an open recording session into a concert; Max Gordon then offered him a band at the Village Vanguard.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Scores from Town Hall and the energy of repeating them
segments.summary: Anger drove the Vanguard music; reusing old scores costs as much energy as writing new ones.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: The Vanguard band, its writing and Buddy Collette's advice
segments.summary: Johnson praises the ten-piece band and its economical writing; Collette told Mingus to leave room for solos.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Monterey, second year: told to get off the stage
segments.summary: After John Handy's set ran long, a stagehand told Mingus to cut it short, so he played one tune.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Don't Be Afraid, The Clown's Afraid Too and Let My Children Hear Music
segments.summary: Johnson on transcribing the Monterey pieces; Mingus on writing the multi-line French horn theme, the 15-measure section.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Revelations and writing six-eight in four-four
segments.summary: The hardest piece he wrote; the Brandeis ensemble with Art Farmer, Bill Evans and others.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Learning to write for harp
segments.summary: Mingus never studied harp writing; a harpist on a poetry date showed him what not to write.

segments.chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
segments.title: Portrait, the Fanny show tune and Charlie Parker's absence
segments.summary: String piece Portrait never released, a singers' show-tune project, and remarks on what Parker would do today.

segments.chapter: Massey Hall, race and the record business
segments.title: How the Massey Hall concert came together
segments.summary: Promoter in Toronto, Celia's role, Mingus's company recording Parker and Dizzy; Bird showed up after all.

segments.chapter: Massey Hall, race and the record business
segments.title: Dizzy pulls a knife on Mingus after Massey Hall
segments.summary: Dizzy resented Mingus getting a solo and pulled a knife; Mingus found the fire ax; similar scene with Juan Tizol.

segments.chapter: Massey Hall, race and the record business
segments.title: Fear of Parker, Dizzy, Bud and Max; drugs and manners
segments.summary: Mingus was wary of the bebop circle's drugs and cursing and only came to love Bird later.

segments.chapter: Massey Hall, race and the record business
segments.title: Ending the session and starting a new tape
segments.summary: Mingus is tired and stops; recording resumes later on a new tape.

segments.chapter: Massey Hall, race and the record business
segments.title: Not evil, paranoid: police in the ghettos
segments.summary: Asked what posterity should know, Mingus talks of being called Evil by Jimmy Rowles, ghetto police and the beating of Max Roach.

segments.chapter: Massey Hall, race and the record business
segments.title: Meditations on Integration and the concentration camps story
segments.summary: Eric Dolphy told him of barbed-wire camps for civil-rights marchers; the piece's original title; the Nazis in America.

segments.chapter: Massey Hall, race and the record business
segments.title: Poor whites enslaved by the same people
segments.summary: Mingus reconsiders blanket anti-white feeling and talks about strikers, miners and Ford.

segments.chapter: Massey Hall, race and the record business
segments.title: Record companies hiding that jazz sells
segments.summary: Festival crowds versus what record companies admit; jazz sells again and again and costs less to make than rock.

segments.chapter: Massey Hall, race and the record business
segments.title: Duke's royalties at Columbia, and the Tizol scene
segments.summary: Ellington's complaint about Columbia royalties; Mingus's few meetings with him and the Tizol scene in his book.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Sidemen who came through his bands: Parlan, Waldron, Knepper, Shaw
segments.summary: Johnson asks about players who benefited from his bands; Clarence Shaw's death and writing.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Dannie Richmond
segments.summary: Mingus says Richmond now leans toward rock but knows his music best; Johnson recalls Richmond guiding him at the Showplace.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Booker Ervin and John Handy on tenor
segments.summary: Ervin's time in the band; Handy's Body and Soul at the Five Spot.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Paul Bley, Eric Dolphy and Ted Curson
segments.summary: Mingus's judgments: Bley partial fit, Dolphy sincere, Curson not serious about music.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Roland Kirk, George Barrow, Jaki Byard and Tommy Turrentine
segments.summary: Short assessments; Kirk used as a tool, Byard rounded out the band.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Why Mingus bands were inimitable; amateurs versus great soloists
segments.summary: Mingus says others copied his arrangements and pedal points, and that his ensemble sound outstripped his soloists.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: How much tape the Smithsonian wants
segments.summary: Talk of the five hours of tape needed and who transcribes it.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Cover versions: Goodbye Pork Pie Hat, Jeff Beck and Woody Herman
segments.summary: Few artists have recorded his songs; Beck's platinum album includes Pork Pie Hat.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Electric guitar, Larry Coryell and John Scofield
segments.summary: Mingus softens on electric instruments and likes Coryell and Scofield from Three or Four Shades of Blues.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: The Philharmonic Hall concert and the ovation
segments.summary: Johnson recalls the huge ovation at Charles Mingus and Friends, and young people's identification with him as a rebel.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Talking with fans and tiring in the interview
segments.summary: Young people do not talk to him; Nat Hentoff will interview him next; illness limits his answers.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Why he wrote long, complex pieces from age 19
segments.summary: Jazz players limited themselves to one tempo and meter; he loved Stravinsky, Debussy, Ravel, Strauss.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Roland Kirk and demanding discipline on the bandstand
segments.summary: Kirk learned his compositions unprompted; Mingus insisted on finesse and ran the band hard.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Six marriages and six children
segments.summary: Music cost him wives; he gives the children's ages.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Dorian Mingus and Jimmy Rowles
segments.summary: Johnson saw Dorian explain himself to Rowles after the quarrel; Dorian is 19.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: The unpublished portion of Beneath the Underdog
segments.summary: Mingus wants Sue to edit the cut material about record-company theft and Debut sales.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Joe Gallo as manager and the Johnny Roberts date
segments.summary: His accountants and attorney had ties to Gallo; Gallo's men scared off a hood who wanted him to record.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Joining Lionel Hampton and the pay dispute
segments.summary: Hampton agreed to $400 a week; Gladys Hampton cut it to $125 on the road in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Hampton's dishonesty, the mileage claim and show music
segments.summary: Jack Kelso collected mileage through the union; Mingus calls Hampton crooked and soulless.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: How High the Moon, Midnight Sun and Fats Navarro
segments.summary: Mingus says he showed Hampton the riffs behind Midnight Sun and was not paid for his charts.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Buying DownBeat polls
segments.summary: Hampton had truckloads of tearsheets bought to win the poll; Mingus put in Red Callender's name.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Nat Hentoff as a classical disc jockey
segments.summary: Mingus claims he got Hentoff into jazz and recalls their letters.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: The Tijuana night in Beneath the Underdog
segments.summary: Johnson asks if it happened as written; Mingus says yes and talks of Dannie Richmond.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: His wives, the shooting and the Bible
segments.summary: Who his first wife was, the book not being scripture, and a Bible joke.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Lalo Schifrin, Dizzy and film work for black musicians
segments.summary: Mingus's paranoia about black players excluded from films and TV; Johnson disagrees about Schifrin.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Royalties: Carla Bley, Brubeck and Paul Desmond
segments.summary: Argument about whether white jazz musicians do better; Johnson says the record business steals from everyone.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Nobody black has made money except Duke
segments.summary: Mingus says no black man is a millionaire and Ellington did not make money from Columbia; Johnson cites Famous Amos.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
segments.title: Mingus ends the first interview
segments.summary: Mingus asks to stop and be done; the first interview ends.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Second interview with Nat Hentoff: why composing matters most
segments.summary: Hentoff asks whether leader, bassist or composer matters most to him; Mingus says composing.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: The decline of real jam sessions
segments.summary: Jam sessions began as release for big-band players; booking agents and Norman Granz turned them into shows.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Bass battles and the best he ever played
segments.summary: He names a San Francisco jam session as his best; Blanton, Slam Stewart and Callender left no competition.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Why Jimmy Blanton mattered, and jazz bass versus classical bass
segments.summary: Blanton played high and low in all keys, unlike Walter Page; a story of a bass player who could not sight-read; classical bass soloists seem simple by comparison.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Seeing Charlie Parker put people down
segments.summary: Mingus lost enthusiasm for playing because there was nowhere to blow; Parker barred a player from the stand and mocked Mel Torme.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Was Charlie Parker well read? His voice
segments.summary: Parker could talk on any subject; Mingus thinks he raised his voice to seem refined.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Birdland night with Bird, Bud Powell and Art Blakey; God and no God
segments.summary: Johnson recalls the collapsed set; Mingus remembers a photo of Bud in Bird's arms and a conversation about God.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Lennie Tristano's coldness
segments.summary: Mingus says the coldness is real and tells a story about Tristano advising a bandmate about his new wife.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Throwing drafts away, unfinished songs and Fables of Faubus lyrics
segments.summary: Composing frees him from interference; words slow his songs; Faubus words came after the music.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Why few jazz musicians write bodies of work
segments.summary: Mingus calls players lazy; Parker wrote blues and new melodies on standard changes.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Ornette Coleman: weak alto but ingenious composer
segments.summary: Mingus doubts his intonation but praises his sense of composition and says many copy him.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: John Coltrane asks where to go next
segments.summary: Coltrane visited him at the Showplace and asked what to do next; Mingus said get out of the rut.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Critics who discover artists
segments.summary: Critics are uncritical of Coltrane after attacking him; who discovered Ornette and Roland Kirk.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Critics never influenced him; not copying yourself
segments.summary: He compares himself to Gauguin, never stylizing, and says Duke did not copy himself.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: What a critic should be, and the danger of Times reviews
segments.summary: Critics should report what happened and review last; one reviewer can kill a play.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Martin Williams, Jelly Roll Morton and Miles Davis again
segments.summary: Mingus again claims priority on one-chord playing, citing the Charles Cros award; Bill Evans and Wynton Kelly taught Miles.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Miles Davis as actor and his rock period
segments.summary: Mingus calls Miles a great bebopper who bluffs and gave the public noise.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Lester Young in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Young was sensitive and warm and put down only Stan Getz.

segments.chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
segments.title: Lester Young's music and pre-Army tapes
segments.summary: Sad music; Dexter Gordon's early tapes show Young swinging hard before the Army beating.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Meeting Sy Johnson at a Boston radio station
segments.summary: Mingus and Johnson recall how they first met when Johnson was a disc jockey and played classical music.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Norman Granz, George Wein and what jazz musicians were paid
segments.summary: Mingus says promoters paid too little, citing his cheap first Jazz at the Philharmonic and Louis Armstrong's guarantee.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Playing with Kid Ory and bassists who could not read
segments.summary: Mingus took any job with music to read; Ory could hardly sight-read bass.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Eddie Gomez plays only high
segments.summary: Mingus likes Gomez but wishes he would use the whole bass.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Working for Kid Ory; Barney Bigard got Ory out of the post office
segments.summary: Mingus was hired by Ory after Barney Bigard, who brought Ory back to playing.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Hampton's underpayment, again
segments.summary: Mingus repeats the $400 versus $125 story and says he was never paid for arrangements.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Hampton's politics and the Rockefeller Attica title
segments.summary: Hampton as a Republican and Rockefeller's man; his Attica piece; Sue to time the tapes.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Ellington's speech captured in Beneath the Underdog
segments.summary: Johnson marvels at Mingus's recall of Duke's mocking elegance in the book; Mingus calls it a spooky talent.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Playing in Ellington's band: Blanton tribute, Hodges and Al Sears
segments.summary: He learned nothing from inside; Duke refused to let him play and never hired a Hodges-like alto player.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Ben Webster's sound and playing without a mike
segments.summary: Webster and Hawkins had the biggest tones; a Stuyvesant Casino gig and playing loud without amplification.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Ben Webster in Europe: dinner talk of gangsters
segments.summary: Webster cared about young musicians but he and McPherson talked only gangsters, Baby Bell and Lucky Luciano.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
segments.title: Hiring Ben Webster and the drunken fight
segments.summary: Webster got drunk on the job and wanted to fight; Mingus ran from him.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Monk on acting crazy; Bud Powell, Bird and Paul Chambers
segments.summary: Monk's remark at Birdland that they should not fall in love with the act; Chambers feigned addiction.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Acts of violence: the gun at Chimbo's and the New York gun
segments.summary: Mingus describes beating a gunman unconscious in San Francisco and the New York gun incident.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Jimmy Knepper, the Town Hall copyist dispute and the open recording session
segments.summary: Mingus gives his version of the Knepper incident and explains the planned open recording session.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Dizzy Gillespie as a person; looking at him in Europe
segments.summary: Dizzy stayed healthy and sweet; he sensed Mingus's love from across a room.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Dizzy's development and Freddy Webster's Stardust
segments.summary: Mingus claims Webster influenced Dizzy and Bird; he heard him with Lunceford with the audience in tears.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Hampton's old-fashioned phrasing
segments.summary: Hampton still plays scales with embellishments; Mingus reminds Johnson of a letter.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Fats Navarro and playing what is happening
segments.summary: Clifford Brown came out of Navarro; Mingus compares playing the moment to ballads.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Studio atmosphere and an A&R man who stays in the booth
segments.summary: Mingus complains that his Atlantic A&R man cannot read scores or listen in the room; he brought Teo Macero in at his own cost.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Why live recording beats studio gimmicks
segments.summary: Live dates avoid gimmicks and retakes, but Atlantic dislikes them; the Showcase date recorded with the lights off.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Recording technology and engineers who read scores
segments.summary: Too many microphones and technology; an engineer should read the score, as Columbia engineers once did.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: His ideal recording team and setting
segments.summary: He would use Teddy Charles, Teo Macero and Les Paul and record in Columbia's church studio with unlimited time.

segments.chapter: Bud, Bird, Dizzy and recording
segments.title: Symphonies and string quartets he never got to; nothing fully worked
segments.summary: He always wanted to write five-movement symphonies and quartets; no piece came out as he wanted and the new Atlantic balance is wrong.

segments.chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
segments.title: Les Koenig's relaxed recording sessions
segments.summary: Johnson contrasts Contemporary Records' open-ended sessions with East Coast practice.

segments.chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
segments.title: A real school of jazz: faculty, students and Paul Jeffries
segments.summary: Mingus says the music is taught mainly to white players, names ideal teachers, and says composition cannot be taught.

segments.chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
segments.title: Black children in Washington who did not know Duke
segments.summary: Black people have no unity or church; federal school money does not reach jazz.

segments.chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
segments.title: Jazz is dead: Monk's illness and the black man owed a living
segments.summary: Mingus insists the American black man's jazz is for the archives, with Dizzy and Monk gone.

segments.chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
segments.title: Convincing Paul Jeffries that Eric Dolphy matched Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Dolphy had a big sound and developed themes; a student set Dolphy against Parker.

segments.chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
segments.title: White students and the future of black jazz
segments.summary: Mingus thinks whites will hold the music and black players will drift to rock, unless a strong new black player emerges.

segments.chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
segments.title: Hamlet Bluiett and George Adams
segments.summary: Mingus hired Bluiett for his sound but found the players could only play out.

segments.chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
segments.title: A player should be an actor: Bird's ballads
segments.summary: Music should contain beauty and ugliness; the player should live each moment as if hearing it first, as Parker did.

segments.chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
segments.title: Duke on avant-garde records, and Ornette's confident upbringing
segments.summary: Ellington declines to go back to avant-garde; Mingus contrasts Ornette's parented confidence with his own struggle for approval.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Duke Ellington's aloofness and calling Mingus king of the waltz
segments.summary: Mingus has few real talks with Duke; a Yale scene with Max Roach, and Duke's Birdland compliment about his waltzes.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Mercer Ellington and the Ellington band after Duke
segments.summary: Mingus says the band should drop Ellington's book; Mercer and his father's coolness toward him.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Why jazz dates rarely used singers: Sarah Vaughan and Billie Holiday
segments.summary: Singers who live the lyrics are hard to find; Billie shocked him with her cursing.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Ivy Anderson and why good jazz singers are scarce
segments.summary: Singers do not go to jam sessions, so they do not learn jazz.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Jam session gatekeepers: Big Bill Moore, Lockjaw Davis and Monk's lateness
segments.summary: Players had to audition to sit in; Monk used to leave while someone filled in.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Praise for a big-sound tenor player who plays ballads
segments.summary: Mingus loves his sound and his ballads, which make people cry.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Dizzy plays warm and loves to jam
segments.summary: Dizzy's clown image hides warm playing; he is a jam-session freak.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Jam sessions in California: Charlie Christian and the Whitman Brothers
segments.summary: He was refused a seat next to Charlie Christian; Joe Comfort's electric bass and Maxwell Davis's playing.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: The Flamingo Club and why jam sessions are dead
segments.summary: Mingus worked at a jam session place; today nobody tries to jam.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Paying sidemen versus Hampton, South American touring and being voodooed
segments.summary: Mingus paid sidemen over $1,000 a week by the night while Hampton paid by the week; his illness and Katherine Dunham.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Where the next improviser comes from; Scott LaFaro at the Showplace
segments.summary: LaFaro slept in a chair at the Showplace; Mingus thinks he started bass playing for its own sake.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Ray Brown, Red Mitchell and melodic bass playing
segments.summary: Brown played exercises; Red Mitchell is the only bassist who plays melodically.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Ella Fitzgerald and Ray Brown; singing without soul
segments.summary: Mingus attacks Ella as cruel and soulless and says Ben Webster beat her; he prefers Dinah Washington.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Breaking the bootleggers and the record business
segments.summary: Musician-owned labels cannot beat big distributors; Mingus plans to bootleg the bootleggers' records.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Reactions to Beneath the Underdog and Louis Lomax
segments.summary: Names he used, fear of some characters, and how the manuscript was copied and spread.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: What the book left out: gangsters, the police and ballroom dancing
segments.summary: Mingus says police and gangsters killed big bands and dancing because dancing caused integration; Half Note harassment.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Not a pimp: Diane, the police brothel and Bellevue
segments.summary: He insists he could not be a pimp and ties his Bellevue stay to Diane, a call girl.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: If he could redo things: pushing the atomic button for a fresh start
segments.summary: Mingus says he would blow up a few places so people could start over with more love.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Death, old ruins and wishing for a good education
segments.summary: He wishes he had had teachers who understood children and a fundamental education.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Wanting to be Leonard Bernstein
segments.summary: He would rather be in the Boston Pops bass section writing, discovering Negro talent like Bernstein.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Wrapping up: Mingus's string quartet
segments.summary: Hentoff has to leave for newspaper strike preparations; Mingus offers his string quartet recording.

segments.chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
segments.title: Pocket-sized bombs, Red Brigades and the Mafia
segments.summary: Idle talk about who knows where the button is, Japanese protesters and the Mafia.

segments.chapter: Retyped duplicate pages
segments.title: Retyped pages: composing first, and the end of jam sessions
segments.summary: Pages 200-212 repeat parts of the second interview; this repeats the composing and jam-session opening.

segments.chapter: Retyped duplicate pages
segments.title: Retyped pages: bass battles and Jimmy Blanton
segments.summary: Repeat of the talk on bass contests and Blanton's technique.

segments.chapter: Retyped duplicate pages
segments.title: Retyped pages: Parker, Birdland and Johnson's radio work
segments.summary: Fragments repeating the Bird and Bud Powell Birdland night and the Boston radio recollection.

segments.chapter: Retyped duplicate pages
segments.title: Retyped pages: Granz, Wein and Hampton's pay
segments.summary: Repeated passages on promoters' pay and Hampton's underpayment.

segments.chapter: Retyped duplicate pages
segments.title: Retyped pages: Dizzy, Freddy Webster and Hampton's phrasing
segments.summary: Repeat of the discussion of Dizzy's playing, Webster's influence and Hampton's phrasing.

segments.chapter: Retyped duplicate pages
segments.title: Retyped pages: Fats Navarro and the Atlantic A&R man
segments.summary: A fragment on Navarro merges with the repeated complaint about the A&R man and Teo Macero.

segments.chapter: Retyped duplicate pages
segments.title: Retyped pages: engineers and the ideal recording team
segments.summary: Repeat of engineers who read scores and Mingus's dream production team in Columbia's church studio.
